analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans exclude unlimited foreign-earned wages from US income tax.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, Americans living and working abroad can exclude only a capped amount of their foreign wages from US income tax. This bill would have removed the cap entirely, letting any American who works abroad pay no US income tax on their wages, no matter how large. It was introduced by an Indiana Republican with 19 cosponsors in July 2006, sent to the tax-writing committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans earning wages abroad, and disproportionately the highest earners among them. The existing exclusion is capped, so a moderately paid teacher overseas already avoids most US tax; removing the cap means the benefit flows to executives, consultants, and finance professionals with large foreign salaries, who could pay zero US income tax on those wages. Employers that send high-paid staff abroad would also find it cheaper, since they would no longer need to cover those employees' US tax bills.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the tax code so that, at a taxpayer's election, all earned income from services performed in a foreign country is excluded from gross income and exempt from US tax, with no dollar limit [S2] [S3].
Pensions, annuities, and pay from the US government or its agencies are carved out, so the exclusion applies to private foreign wages rather than federal salaries [S3].
It would take effect for tax years beginning after enactment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: US taxpayers who remain in the domestic tax base. Every dollar of wages removed from taxation by Americans abroad has to be made up by other taxpayers, through higher deficits or higher taxes on people who cannot move their earning abroad. The gain scales with income, so the largest winners are the wealthiest expatriates while the cost spreads across everyone else.

drawbacks.text: The revenue cost lands entirely on people who stay in the US tax base: a worker earning the same money in Ohio pays full income tax while an identical worker in Zurich would pay none, which shifts the burden and rewards moving earnings offshore [S3].

Because the exclusion is unlimited, the benefit concentrates at the top — someone already under the current cap gains nothing, while a seven-figure foreign salary avoids hundreds of thousands of dollars in tax, increasing inequality in the tax system [S2] [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the direct revenue loss to the Treasury at a time of large federal deficits, and the risk of encouraging income to be routed through foreign employers or contracts [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real, narrow benefit: it removes a genuine tax penalty on smaller numbers of Americans abroad and could make US workers slightly easier to place overseas. But because the exclusion would be unlimited, nearly all the value goes to high earners, and the cost is shifted onto domestic taxpayers and the deficit. The design is upside down for a bill titled 'Working American Competitiveness' — a low-earner abroad gets almost nothing, while a wealthy expatriate gets everything.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee in July 2006, never received a hearing or a floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Chocola introduced the bill on July 28, 2006, with 19 Republican cosponsors listed on the original text [S1] [S3] [S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee that writes tax law [S1] [S5].
No further action was recorded — no markup, no vote, no companion Senate activity — and the bill died there when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Domestic taxpayers and the Treasury are better off, because an unlimited tax carve-out for high-earning Americans abroad was never enacted; the tax base stayed intact. Had it passed, the largest gains would have gone to wealthy expatriates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Domestic taxpayers; the tax base stayed intact

for.name: Rep. Chris Chocola
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to remove the limit on the foreign earned income exclusion.

for.name: 19 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, joining as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remaining five months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never advanced far enough for a recorded vote [S4] [S5].

industries.note: They would pay zero US income tax on unlimited foreign wages, with the benefit concentrated at the top since earners below the existing cap gain little. The cost of the carve-out falls on domestic taxpayers [S2] [S3].

Companies posting high-paid staff overseas would no longer need to compensate them for US tax on foreign earnings, making overseas assignments cheaper. The saving would flow mainly to the employer and the executive, not to ordinary workers [S3].
